name: Sara Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential, so you can separate your public line from what you believe privately. What does an ordinary workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Sara, 43, and I’m a junior developer at a company that makes software for workshop bookings. I earned a two-year college diploma after working in a parts shop, and I still need a senior person to check my harder code changes. I start with failed bookings, ask the workshop what happened, then fix and test the form. I use AI every day to suggest tests and explain logs, but I check its answer against the booking record.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is at stake for your household?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner, Marco, is an electrician. We have two children in school and a mortgage, with about four months of expenses saved. My pay is typical for a developer, and there are some similar jobs nearby. I like useful risks, but I know the mortgage will not accept a clever idea in place of money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team AI Plateau looks like the assistant we already use: handy for tests, not the person who answers to a workshop. I would keep asking whether a suggested fix matches a real booking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I would feel fairly secure about my pay and Marco’s electrical work. I still worry about being junior when a bad booking reaches a customer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep using AI for test suggestions and check each one against an actual failed booking. I’d transfer 250 monthly into our mortgage reserve while both wages hold. In the first year I’d ask the senior developer to review one tricky form fix with me every Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about my own learning curve, though I expect our income to stay. I can use a tool without trusting it blindly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What was a booking mistake you caught?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A workshop once booked two lifts at the same hour because our form ignored a blocked slot. The printed workshop schedule exposed a double-booking our code missed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you talk about your work with the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show the children how a real schedule exposes a software mistake. They enjoy seeing what I do, even when I get it wrong first.

say: I see **AI Plateau** as test help that still needs workshop checks.
I would compare each suggested fix with a **real booking**.
think: I expect our **two incomes** to stay steady in this mild picture.
I worry my **junior mistakes** could still reach a customer.
do: **Keep** using AI test suggestions and checking failed workshop bookings.
**Transfer** 250 monthly into the mortgage reserve while both wages hold.
**Review** one tricky form fix with a senior developer each Friday.
feel: **Uneasy** about my learning curve, with household income likely stable.
S0.quote: The printed workshop schedule exposed a double-booking our code missed.
fieldNote: Her **parts-shop experience** helps her test code against workshop schedules.
She uses **AI daily** but expects steady wages; the mortgage reserve grows only while both incomes hold.

steps.text: Keep testing AI suggestions against failed workshop bookings
Transfer 250 monthly into mortgage savings while both wages hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption will let software answer booking questions and draft repairs to our code. I would tell the team to publish the mistakes it catches before removing a person from the review.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect junior developers like me to lose hours if one senior person can supervise several AI tools. Marco’s wiring work may change later, but it will not replace my lost pay soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d compare the assistant with fifteen old double-booking faults this month and teach our workshop clients to flag a wrong slot. I’d use a free evening class on system testing if Marco can cover the children on Tuesdays. In the first year, if management cuts junior hours, I’d look at actual testing vacancies nearby rather than resign first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because a cut in my hours would make the mortgage tighter. I have four months saved and fifteen old booking faults to test, not a guarantee of another job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you change at home if hours fall?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Marco we should pause the planned fence repair if my hours fall. I would not give up the children’s school transport to protect a garden fence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What evidence would you show your manager?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would write down the fifteen faults and show my manager which ones the assistant missed. If it passes, I would let it draft more tests but keep a human sign-off.

say: I expect **Steady Disruption** to speed booking replies and code fixes.
I would publish **caught mistakes** before removing human review.
think: I expect **junior hours** may shrink under one senior AI supervisor.
I cannot rely on Marco’s **electrical pay** to replace my income.
do: **Test** the assistant against fifteen old double-booking faults this month.
**Attend** a free testing class if Marco covers Tuesday childcare.
**Check** actual local testing vacancies if junior hours are cut.
feel: **Anxious** about reduced hours and the mortgage, with four months saved.
S1.quote: I have four months saved and fifteen old booking faults to test, not a guarantee of another job.
fieldNote: Her **daily AI use** makes her willing to test, while junior standing leaves hours exposed.
Her **evening class** needs Marco’s childcare, and a job search waits on real cuts and vacancies.

steps.text: Keep using AI for workshop tests and compare fifteen past double-booking faults
Attend free system-testing class if Marco covers Tuesday childcare
Check actual local testing vacancies if junior hours are cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the workshop team AGI by 2028 can do our booking-code thinking work by 2028. Robots for hands-on electrical tasks come around 2031, so Marco’s work has more time than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect my junior coding role to end or shrink sharply. Four months of savings will not carry a mortgage for long, even if Marco’s jobs continue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d stop our planned kitchen cabinet purchase and hold the cash. I’d ask my employer for written notice and any paid transition time, then list real workshop support openings. In the first year after 2028, if I lose my job, I’d apply to those actual vacancies and use savings only for mortgage and essentials.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I think my income could disappear before we can build a larger reserve, while the children still need a steady home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Marco about the kitchen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The old kitchen cabinets can stay; we need to know our next payslips before buying new ones. I would tell Marco we must keep money for his work van’s safety checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What family help could you really ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask my brother if he could watch the children during interviews, if his shifts permit. I would not ask him to pay our mortgage.

say: I expect **AGI by 2028** to reach workshop code before electrical robots arrive.
I would tell colleagues Marco’s **hands-on work** has about three more years.
think: I expect my **junior role** to end or shrink sharply.
Our **four-month reserve** would drain quickly under the mortgage.
do: **Cancel** the kitchen cabinet purchase and keep cash for essentials now.
**Request** written notice and paid transition time from my employer.
**Apply** for actual workshop support openings if dismissed after 2028.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected lost income and a limited mortgage cushion.
S2.quote: The old kitchen cabinets can stay; we need to know our next payslips before buying new ones.
fieldNote: She locates her **code risk** in 2028 and Marco’s hands-on robot exposure around 2031.
She would ask her **brother for childcare**, conditional on his shifts, and would not treat him as a lender.

steps.text: Cancel planned kitchen cabinets and hold cash for mortgage essentials
Apply for real workshop support vacancies if dismissed after 2028
Ask her brother for interview childcare if his shifts allow

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives us five years to understand what workshops still need from software. Thinking AI reaches our code in 2031; robots for electrical work follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still expect my coding hours may vanish. Five years lets me practise a different service while Marco’s work and my wage still support the household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d try a Saturday service setting up appointment calendars for two local repair shops, charging a small fixed fee only if they like the trial. Marco would cover the children on trial Saturdays only if his electrical work allows. In the first year after 2031, I’d continue only if repeat fees cover travel and childcare and justify time away from the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my developer job, but I can test a second income without betting the mortgage. The two repair shops may not want my Saturday calendar service at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What number would make the Saturday work worthwhile?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would write down what each shop paid and how many Saturday hours it took. If repeat fees do not cover travel and childcare or justify time away from the children, I would stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would handle childcare on trial days?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marco would take the children on those two trial Saturdays if his electrical work allows. I would not book a third shop before we know whether the first two pay.

say: I see **AGI by 2031** as time to test paid workshop service.
I know **2034 robots** follow the earlier code change.
think: I expect my **coding hours** may disappear by 2031.
I can trial **Saturday work** while wages continue, without assuming customers exist.
do: **Trial** calendar setup for two repair shops if Marco can cover the children.
**Charge** only if the shops accept the trial and keep a record of hours and costs.
**Continue** after 2031 only if repeat fees cover travel, childcare and family time.
feel: **Anxious** about coding pay, with a limited second-income test.
S3.quote: The two repair shops may not want my Saturday calendar service at all.
fieldNote: She treats **customer demand** as unknown and limits the trial to two Saturdays without a loan.
The **continuation gate** requires repeat fees to cover travel and childcare and justify time away from her children.

steps.text: Trial calendar setup for two shops if Marco can cover childcare
Continue after 2031 only if repeat fees cover travel, childcare and family time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2036 gives a decade to improve our booking system and the shops it serves. Thinking AI reaches my code in 2036, with electrical robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I can build useful work by then, but I would not sign the family up for debt on a forecast. My junior job still needs practice today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep fixing booking forms with senior review and use AI each week to test the slots our clients complain about. I’d teach one neighbour’s apprentice the booking system on a free Saturday once a quarter. In the first year after 2036, if coding work has shrunk, I’d ask the two shops whether paid calendar help still makes sense before offering it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about my junior role over a decade, but our current pay and savings give us room to choose. I would rather test a real customer need than buy a grand plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why teach the apprentice for free?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the apprentice lesson free because I learned the parts trade from people who did that for me. I could not take on weekly classes alongside my children and mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a shop has no budget after 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a shop has no budget for calendar help after 2036, I would keep looking at actual developer openings. I would not buy software subscriptions to chase a non-paying customer.

say: I see **AGI by 2036** as time to improve booking work and local shops.
I know **2039 robots** follow the earlier coding change.
think: I can build **useful work** without borrowing against a forecast.
I still need **coding practice** despite the long horizon.
do: **Keep** fixing booking forms with senior review and weekly AI slot tests.
**Teach** a neighbour’s apprentice the system once a quarter for free.
**Ask** two shops about paid calendar work after 2036; search developer vacancies if coding shrinks and they lack budget.
feel: **Uneasy** about the longer future, with current wages and savings intact.
S4.quote: I would rather test a real customer need than buy a grand plan.
fieldNote: She keeps the **long horizon** grounded in current coding practice and no household debt.
Her **free apprentice lessons** fit family time; future calendar work depends on shops still paying.

steps.text: Keep fixing booking forms with senior review and weekly AI tests
Search actual developer vacancies after 2036 if coding shrinks and shops lack budget

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my junior code income could end before we can save much more. Written notice, paid transition time and actual workshop vacancies would help. My brother could watch the children for an interview, but he cannot become our income plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who has to tell a mechanic a machine booked two cars into one lift. A customer sees the booking screen, but the mechanic has to solve a double-booked lift.

headlineQuote: A customer sees the booking screen, but the mechanic has to solve a double-booked lift.
portrait: Sara is a **43-year-old junior developer** with a two-year diploma, typical pay and four months of expenses saved.
She uses **AI daily** on workshop-booking faults, checking suggestions against schedules from her earlier parts-shop work.
Her partner’s **electrical work** faces hands-on robots about three years after thinking AI threatens her code.
She tests **two paid-shop trials** without loans and asks family only for conditional interview childcare.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her junior income before the household has a larger mortgage reserve.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, paid transition time and actual workshop openings would help.
